items.stimulus:
Peat is a dark, spongy soil made of plant material that has only partly decayed. It forms in places where the ground stays waterlogged for most of the year. Under water, oxygen is scarce, and the microbes that normally break down dead leaves and stems work very slowly. As a result, each year's growth is not fully recycled, and a thin layer of organic matter is added to the deposit. Peat typically accumulates at around a millimetre a year or less, so a deposit several metres deep may represent many thousands of years of growth.

Peatlands are found from the Arctic to the tropics. In cool northern regions many are bogs dominated by sphagnum mosses, which hold large amounts of water and make their surroundings acidic, further slowing decay. Bogs receive their water mainly from rain, whereas fens are fed by groundwater and streams and usually support a wider range of plants. In South-East Asia and parts of South America, much peat forms beneath swamp forests.

Although peatlands cover only around three per cent of the world's land, commonly cited estimates suggest that they hold roughly a third of all the carbon stored in soils. That carbon stays locked away only as long as the peat remains wet. When peatlands are drained for farming, forestry or fuel, air enters the upper layers, decomposition speeds up, and carbon is released to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. Drained peat also burns easily, and fires can smoulder underground for weeks, spreading smoke over wide areas.

For this reason, restoration projects increasingly aim to block drainage ditches and raise water tables again. Rewetting usually reduces carbon dioxide emissions quickly, but it can increase releases of methane, another greenhouse gas, especially in the first few years. Researchers therefore judge restoration by its overall effect over several decades rather than by a single season's measurements, and most studies so far suggest that keeping peat wet is better for the climate than leaving it drained.

items.stimulus:
For centuries, people have described seeing glowing spheres drift through the air during thunderstorms. Accounts of this phenomenon, known as ball lightning, are broadly consistent: the ball is usually somewhere between the size of a tennis ball and that of a football, glows steadily in white, yellow, orange or red, and lasts from a second or two to perhaps ten seconds. It may float horizontally rather than fall, and some witnesses report it passing through a closed window or entering a room down a chimney. It disappears either silently or with a sharp bang. Because these events are brief, rare and unpredictable, for a long time almost all the evidence came from eyewitnesses, and some scientists doubted that the phenomenon existed at all.

Several explanations compete. One of the most discussed proposes that when lightning strikes the ground, it vaporises minerals in the soil. Silicon released in this way could condense into a cloud of tiny particles that burn slowly as they combine with oxygen in the air, producing a glowing ball. Laboratory experiments in which an electric arc was passed through thin wafers of silicon have produced luminous balls lasting several seconds, which supporters regard as encouraging. A second family of explanations suggests that the ball is a pocket of energy sustained by microwaves generated in the storm; this could account for reports of balls appearing inside aircraft or passing through glass, which the soil hypothesis struggles to explain. A third view holds that some sightings are not external objects at all: the intense, rapidly changing magnetic field near a lightning strike may stimulate the visual areas of an observer's brain, producing the impression of a glowing shape.

In 2012, researchers in China who were studying ordinary lightning happened to film a ball lightning event and record the spectrum of its light. The ball lasted under two seconds, and its light contained the signatures of silicon, iron and calcium, elements that are common in soil. Many commentators saw this as strong support for the soil hypothesis. Others cautioned that a single recording cannot show that every case has the same cause, and that what witnesses call ball lightning may in fact be several different phenomena sharing one name.

items.stimulus:
A festival can only be held on the same day each year if a community agrees on what a year is, and different traditions have answered that question differently. The cycle of the moon's phases, from one new moon to the next, takes about twenty-nine and a half days, so twelve lunar months add up to roughly 354 days. The solar year, which governs the seasons, is about 365 and a quarter days long. The gap of around eleven days is small in any one year but quickly adds up.

Calendars that follow the moon alone simply accept this drift. The Islamic calendar is the best-known example. Its months begin with the sighting of the new crescent moon, and because its year is shorter than the solar year, the month of Ramadan falls about eleven days earlier each year by the Gregorian reckoning, passing through every season over a cycle of roughly thirty-three years. A fast that falls in the long days of summer in one decade will fall in the short days of winter some years later.

Lunisolar calendars take a different approach: they insert an extra month from time to time so that the months stay roughly in step with the seasons. The Hebrew calendar adds a month in seven years out of every nineteen, which keeps Passover in spring. The traditional Chinese calendar uses a similar scheme, so Lunar New Year always falls between 21 January and 20 February.

Even some festivals in the solar Gregorian calendar depend on the moon. Easter is calculated from a full moon close to the northern spring equinox, which is why it can fall on any Sunday across a span of about five weeks. Christmas, by contrast, is fixed by the solar calendar alone.

These differences are not merely technical. A festival tied to the seasons can carry meanings linked to harvest or renewal, while one that moves through the year may be valued precisely because, over a lifetime, it is kept in every season. Neither system is simply more accurate than the other; each keeps faith with a different cycle in the sky.

items.stimulus:
In 1989 a British epidemiologist noticed something curious in data on thousands of children: those with several older brothers and sisters were less likely to develop hay fever than those who were the first or only child in their family. The idea became known as the hygiene hypothesis.

Later research supported part of the picture. Children who grow up on traditional farms, in close daily contact with livestock and stables, have repeatedly been found to have lower rates of asthma and hay fever than other children living in the same region. Studies of the immune system suggest that early exposure to a wide variety of microbes helps train the body's defences to distinguish real threats from harmless substances such as pollen.

Other findings did not fit so neatly. Many common childhood infections have not been shown to protect against allergies, and asthma is widespread in some poor urban neighbourhoods where infections remain frequent. Many researchers therefore now prefer an 'old friends' version of the idea. On this view, what matters is not illness but regular contact with the largely harmless microbes found in soil, animals and other people, which humans have lived alongside throughout their evolution. Modern life may reduce this contact through city living, caesarean births, antibiotic use and diets low in fibre, although the contribution of each factor is still debated.

The popular name has caused some confusion. Public health experts stress that the evidence gives no reason to stop washing hands or cleaning kitchens, since these habits prevent infections that are dangerous in their own right and have little to do with the varied microbial contact that the theory emphasises. For much of the twentieth century, comics in the English-speaking world were sold as cheap, thin magazines and widely regarded as entertainment for children. The idea that a long, self-contained story told in pictures could be read and reviewed like a novel took decades to gain ground. The term graphic novel was used occasionally in the 1960s, but it reached a wider audience after 1978, when an American cartoonist put it on the cover of a collection of stories about tenement life in New York, partly in the hope that bookshops rather than newsagents would stock it.

The real turning point came in the mid-1980s. Within a short period, several book-length works appeared that treated serious subjects with formal ambition, among them a memoir of the Holocaust in which different peoples are drawn as different animals. Newspapers ran articles announcing that comics had grown up, and in 1992 that memoir received a special Pulitzer Prize. Over the following decades, autobiographical and journalistic works multiplied, translations of Japanese manga found large new readerships among teenagers, and libraries and schools began collecting graphic novels in significant numbers.

The label itself remains contested. Some creators welcome it because it signals that a work deserves the kind of attention given to literary fiction. Others regard it as a marketing term that flatters one format while quietly implying that ordinary comics are inferior. They also point out that many celebrated graphic novels are in fact memoirs, histories or collections of episodes first published in instalments, rather than novels at all.

What seems clearer is that the change in status has altered how such works are made. Because a book can stay in print and on library shelves for years, creators can plan long narratives with careful structure rather than writing for a monthly issue that will soon be thrown away. The form's growing respectability has therefore encouraged exactly the kind of ambitious work that earned it respect in the first place.

items.stimulus:
Rates of reported anxiety and depression among teenagers rose in a number of wealthy countries from the early 2010s, around the time that smartphones and social media became part of most young people's daily lives. To some researchers the timing is telling. They argue that hours spent scrolling have displaced sleep, exercise and face-to-face friendship, and that constant comparison with carefully edited images of peers is particularly harmful to girls in early adolescence.

Others are unconvinced. They point out that a rise occurring at the same time as a new technology does not show that one caused the other; rising academic pressure, growing economic insecurity and a greater willingness to report mental health problems also occurred over the same period. When large surveys are analysed, the association between time spent on social media and wellbeing is usually negative but small, accounting for only a modest share of the differences between individuals. It is also unclear in which direction the influence runs, since young people who are already unhappy may turn to their phones more often.

Part of the disagreement arises because social media use covers very different activities. Sending messages to close friends, watching videos alone late at night and posting photographs for strangers to rate are unlikely to have the same effects. Studies that measure only total screen time may therefore hide harmful and helpful uses that cancel each other out. Experiments in which participants agree to cut back their use for several weeks have produced mixed results, and most have involved university students rather than younger teenagers.

Despite this uncertainty, several governments have moved to restrict children's access to social media, arguing that waiting for conclusive evidence would mean waiting too long. Critics of such measures reply that restrictions may be hard to enforce and could cut isolated young people off from sources of support. On one point most researchers agree: better data, including information that the platforms themselves hold, would help settle the question.

items.stimulus:
In many towns of medieval Europe, people who practised the same craft, such as weaving, baking or metalworking, joined together in associations known as guilds. From around the twelfth century these bodies gained considerable power. A guild might set standards for materials and workmanship, inspect goods, fix the hours of work and limit who could open a workshop in the town. Guilds also served social and religious purposes: members paid into common funds that helped widows and the sick, attended one another's funerals and honoured a patron saint.

Entry to a craft usually began with apprenticeship. A boy, or occasionally a girl, was bound by contract to a master for a fixed number of years, often seven, although terms varied by trade and place. The apprentice lived in the master's household and received food, lodging and instruction rather than wages, and the family frequently paid the master a fee at the start. On completing the term, the young worker became a journeyman, free to work for wages for any master. In some regions, particularly in German-speaking lands, journeymen were expected to travel from town to town for several years, gaining experience of different workshops. To become a master, a journeyman might have to produce a masterpiece, a piece of work judged by senior members of the guild, and pay an entry fee.

Historians disagree about how to judge this system. Some emphasise that guilds protected the interests of existing masters: high fees, long training and preferential treatment for masters' sons kept competition down and prices up. Others argue that, in an age without formal technical schools, long apprenticeships were a practical way of passing on complex skills, and that inspections gave customers some assurance of quality. Both views find support in the surviving records, and the balance probably differed from one town and trade to another. It seems fairer, then, to treat guilds neither as simple monopolies nor as benevolent schools, but as institutions that combined both roles in varying degrees.

items.stimulus:
Most criminal courts treat an offence as a wrong against the state: the prosecution and the defence present their cases, and a judge or magistrate decides the outcome. Victims usually appear, if at all, as witnesses. Restorative justice starts from a different question. Instead of asking only which law was broken and what punishment fits, it asks who was harmed and what can be done to repair that harm.

The best-known restorative practice is the conference. A trained facilitator brings together the person who committed the offence, the person harmed, and supporters of each, such as family members or friends. Each participant describes what happened and how it affected them, and the group then tries to agree on a plan, which might include an apology, payment for damage, or work for the victim or the community. Conferences are normally used only when the offender has admitted responsibility, and participation by the victim is voluntary. In 1989 New Zealand made family group conferences a central part of its youth justice system, and similar schemes have since been adopted in parts of Australia, the United Kingdom and elsewhere, sometimes alongside a court sentence and sometimes in place of prosecution.

Supporters point to evidence from controlled trials. Victims who take part in conferences generally report greater satisfaction with how their case was handled than those whose cases go through court alone, and many say they feel less fearful of the offender afterwards. Effects on reoffending are more modest. On average, offenders who attend conferences commit somewhat fewer crimes in the following years, although results vary considerably between studies, and some reviews have found larger benefits for violent offences than for property offences.

Critics raise several concerns. Some victims may feel pressure to attend or to forgive. An offender who is fluent and confident may appear more remorseful than one who is shy, which could lead to unequal outcomes for similar offences. Others worry that informal schemes can draw into the justice system minor matters that would otherwise have been dropped. Supporters respond that careful screening and well-trained facilitators can address most of these problems, while accepting that the quality of any scheme depends heavily on its resources and training.

items.stimulus:
A consumer price index, or CPI, is designed to answer a simple-sounding question: how much more does it cost today to buy the same things that households bought in an earlier period? Statisticians begin by deciding what belongs in the basket of goods and services. They use surveys of household spending to identify what people buy and how much of their budget goes on each category, such as food, rent, transport, clothing and health care. These shares become the weights of the index. If households spend ten times as much on rent as on bread, a given percentage rise in rents will move the index ten times as much as the same percentage rise in bread prices.

Each period, price collectors record the prices of thousands of specific items in shops, online and from service providers. The changes are combined using the weights, and the result is expressed relative to a base period, usually set equal to 100. An index of 112 therefore means that the basket costs 12 per cent more than it did in the base period.

Keeping the basket fixed makes comparisons straightforward but creates problems. When the price of one product rises sharply, many households switch to cheaper alternatives, so a fixed basket may overstate how much their actual cost of living has risen. Statistical agencies reduce this effect by updating the weights regularly. Changes in quality cause further difficulty: if a new laptop costs the same as last year's model but is much faster, its price has in a sense fallen, and agencies use various methods to adjust for such improvements.

A national CPI also describes an average household that may resemble few real ones. Retired people, renters and families with young children spend their money in different ways, so the same index can understate the price rises faced by some groups and overstate those faced by others. For this reason, some agencies also publish separate indexes for particular types of household. Even so, the headline figure remains widely used, including to adjust pensions and wages and to guide decisions on interest rates.

items.stimulus:
Removing salt from seawater is technically straightforward but has always been expensive, chiefly because of the energy it requires. Two broad families of methods are used today. Thermal methods imitate the natural water cycle: seawater is heated until it evaporates, and the vapour, which leaves the salt behind, is condensed as fresh water. Membrane methods, of which reverse osmosis is by far the most common, instead push seawater at high pressure through a membrane whose pores let water molecules through but hold back most dissolved salts.

For decades thermal plants dominated, especially in parts of the Middle East, where they could be built next to power stations and use heat that would otherwise be wasted. Over the past few decades, however, reverse osmosis has overtaken them and now accounts for most of the world's desalination capacity. The main reason is efficiency. A modern seawater reverse osmosis plant typically uses around three to four kilowatt-hours of electricity per cubic metre of fresh water, including the energy for pumping water in and out, whereas thermal plants use several times as much energy once their heat demand is counted. Much of the improvement has come from devices that capture the pressure remaining in the concentrated salty water leaving the membranes and use it to pressurise incoming seawater.

There is a limit to such gains. Physics sets a minimum amount of energy needed to separate salt from water, and the best plants already operate at only a small multiple of it. Further large cuts in energy use are therefore unlikely to come from better membranes alone. Water that is only slightly salty, such as some groundwater, needs far less energy to treat, because there is less salt to remove.

Energy is not the only cost. Desalination plants produce large volumes of brine, which must be discharged carefully to avoid harming marine life near the outfall, and building a plant requires substantial investment. For these reasons desalination tends to make most sense where cheaper options, such as reducing leaks, recycling wastewater or tapping new freshwater sources, have already been used, or where droughts make conventional supplies unreliable.

Membrane methods, of which reverse osmosis is by far the most common, instead push seawater at high pressure through a membrane whose pores let water molecules through but hold back most dissolved salts.

For decades thermal plants dominated, especially in parts of the Middle East, where they could be built next to power stations and use heat that would otherwise be wasted. Over the past few decades, however, reverse osmosis has overtaken them and now accounts for most of the world's desalination capacity. The main reason is efficiency. A modern seawater reverse osmosis plant typically uses around three to four kilowatt-hours of electricity per cubic metre of fresh water, including the energy for pumping water in and out, whereas thermal plants use several times as much energy once their heat demand is counted. Much of the improvement has come from devices that capture the pressure remaining in the concentrated salty water leaving the membranes and use it to pressurise incoming seawater.

There is a limit to such gains. Physics sets a minimum amount of energy needed to separate salt from water, and the best plants already operate at only a small multiple of it. Further large cuts in energy use are therefore unlikely to come from better membranes alone. Water that is only slightly salty, such as some groundwater, needs far less energy to treat, because there is less salt to remove.

Energy is not the only cost. Desalination plants produce large volumes of brine, which must be discharged carefully to avoid harming marine life near the outfall, and building a plant requires substantial investment. For these reasons desalination tends to make most sense where cheaper options, such as reducing leaks, recycling wastewater or tapping new freshwater sources, have already been used, or where droughts make conventional supplies unreliable.

items.stimulus:
Some university students take prescription medicines intended for conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder or sleep disorders, in the hope of studying longer or performing better in examinations. Surveys in several countries suggest that a minority of students have tried this, although estimates vary widely depending on how the questions are asked. The practice raises both practical and ethical questions.

The practical evidence is less impressive than the drugs' reputation. In healthy people, such medicines appear to produce small improvements on some tasks, particularly those requiring sustained attention, and little or no benefit on others. Several studies have found that users feel more confident and motivated, which may lead them to believe that the drugs help more than they do. Side effects, including disturbed sleep, a raised heart rate and anxiety, are a further concern, and long-term effects in healthy users have been studied very little.

The ethical debate would remain even if a drug were proven safe and effective. One argument holds that enhancement is unfair in the same way as banned substances in sport: a student who uses a drug gains an advantage that others lack. A second argument concerns pressure. If enhancement became common in a competitive course, students who would prefer not to take drugs might feel that they had no real choice. A third asks whether results achieved with chemical help are fully the person's own, although critics reply that every achievement depends on some outside support.

Universities have responded in different ways. A few have classed the non-medical use of prescription stimulants during assessment as academic misconduct, while others treat it mainly as a health issue and focus on educating students about the risks.
